# Binary-choice models {#binary-choice-models}

**Prerequisites.** Conditional probability, Bernoulli variables, linear regression, and maximum-likelihood estimation.

**After working through this chapter, you should be able to:**

- Explain why a linear probability model has heteroskedastic disturbances and potentially inadmissible fitted values.
- Interpret probit and logit models through conditional probabilities and latent variables.
- Write and maximize the likelihood of a binary-choice model.
- Compute and interpret marginal effects.
- Compare models using likelihood-based measures and assess predictions with classification rates and ROC curves.

**Roadmap.** We start from the linear probability model and then introduce nonlinear probability functions. A latent-variable representation motivates probit and logit specifications. The remaining sections cover estimation, marginal effects, goodness of fit, and predictive evaluation before the exercises in Section \@ref(binary-exercises).

Many economic outcomes are qualitative rather than continuous: a household defaults or does not, an individual participates or does not, and a firm enters a market or stays out. When $y_i\in\{0,1\}$, the object to model is the conditional probability $\mathbb{P}(y_i=1\mid\bv{x}_i)$. The covariates are collected in a $K\times1$ vector $\bv{x}_i$.

Examples include participation in the labour force, market entry, and the occurrence of a credit default. A binary outcome need not represent a deliberate choice.

We specify a Bernoulli model:
\begin{equation}
y_i | \bv{X} \sim \mathcal{B}(g(\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta)).
\end{equation}
where $g(\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta)$ is the parameter of the Bernoulli distribution. In other words, conditionally on $\bv{X}$:
\begin{equation}
y_i = \left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
1 & \mbox{ with probability } g(\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\\
0 & \mbox{ with probability } 1-g(\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta),
\end{array}
\right.(\#eq:genericBinary)
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol\theta$ is a vector of parameters to be estimated.

An estimation strategy is to assume that $g(\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta)$ can be proxied by $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}'\bv{x}_i$ and to run a linear regression to estimate $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ (a situation called **Linear Probability Model, LPM**):
$$
y_i = \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}'\bv{x}_i + \varepsilon_i.
$$
If the conditional probability is truly linear, OLS consistently estimates its coefficients; if it is nonlinear, OLS instead estimates the coefficients of the best linear projection. The fitted values can fall below zero or above one. Moreover, because $\mathbb{V}ar(y_i\mid\bv{x}_i)=p_i(1-p_i)$, the disturbances are generally heteroskedastic, so heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors should be used. The disturbances cannot be conditionally Gaussian because $y_i\in\{0,1\}$.



Figure \@ref(fig:LPM) uses simulated observations to compare the linear fit with the probability function that generated the data. A straight line cannot flatten towards both zero and one.

```{r LPM, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="A linear fit and the true probability in a simulated sample of 100 observations. The generating probability is $\\Phi(0.5+2x)$, with standard normal covariates.", fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, out.width="95%"}
local({
  x <- rnorm(100)
  y <- rbinom(100, 1, pnorm(0.5 + 2*x))
  fit <- lm(y ~ x)
  grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out=400)
  par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
  plot(x, y, pch=16, col=adjustcolor("#334155", .45),
       xlim=c(-3,3), ylim=c(-.35,1.35), xlab="Covariate x",
       ylab="Outcome / probability", las=1)
  abline(h=c(0,1), col="#CBD5E1", lty=3)
  lines(grid, predict(fit, data.frame(x=grid)), col="#C76D36", lwd=2)
  lines(grid, pnorm(.5+2*grid), col="#147D92", lwd=2)
  legend("topleft", c("Linear fit", "True probability"),
         col=c("#C76D36", "#147D92"), lwd=2, bty="n", cex=.9)
})
```

Nonlinear models instead map an index $z_i=\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i$ into a probability $p_i=g(z_i)$. Table \@ref(tab:foo) gives common choices. Here $\Phi$ and $\phi$ denote the standard normal distribution and density functions.

Table: (\#tab:foo) Probability functions and their derivatives. The linear specification is included for comparison.

| Model | $g(z)$ | $g'(z)$ |
|-------|--------|---------|
| Probit | $\Phi(z)$ | $\phi(z)$ |
| Logit | $[1+\exp(-z)]^{-1}$ | $g(z)[1-g(z)]$ |
| Complementary log-log | $1-\exp[-\exp(z)]$ | $\exp[z-\exp(z)]$ |
| Linear (LPM) | $z$ | $1$ |

The **probit** and **logit** models use, respectively,
\begin{equation}
g(z)=\Phi(z), (\#eq:probit)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
g(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z)}. (\#eq:logit)
\end{equation}
Both keep probabilities between zero and one. Their coefficients have different scales, so comparisons should focus on predicted probabilities and marginal effects. The complementary log-log link is asymmetric (Figure \@ref(fig:ProbLogit)).

```{r ProbLogit, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Three links from an index to a probability. Probit and logit are symmetric around zero; the complementary log-log link is asymmetric.", fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, out.width="95%"}
local({
  z <- seq(-5,5,length.out=500)
  par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
  plot(z, pnorm(z), type="l", lwd=2, col="#147D92", las=1,
       xlab="Index z", ylab="Probability", ylim=c(0,1))
  lines(z, plogis(z), col="#C76D36", lwd=2, lty=2)
  lines(z, -expm1(-exp(z)), col="#765D9C", lwd=2, lty=3)
  legend("topleft", c("Probit", "Logit", "Complementary log-log"),
         col=c("#147D92", "#C76D36", "#765D9C"), lty=1:3,
         lwd=2, bty="n", cex=.9)
})
```

## Latent-variable and utility interpretations {#latent}

Probability functions specify how covariates map into observed choices. A latent-variable representation supplies an economic interpretation: the observed binary outcome records whether an unobserved index crosses a threshold.

The probit model has an interpretation in terms of latent variables, which, in turn, is often exploited  in structural models, called **Random Utility Models (RUM)**. In such structural models, it is assumed that the agents that have to take the decision do so by selecting the outcome that provides them with the larger utility (for agent $i$, two possible outcomes: $y_i=0$ or $y_i=1$). Part of this utility is observed by the econometrician ---it depends on the covariates $\bv{x}_i$--- and part of it is latent.

In the probit model, we have:
$$
\mathbb{P}(y_i=1|\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta) = \Phi(\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i) = \mathbb{P}(-\varepsilon_{i}<\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i),
$$
where $\varepsilon_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. That is:
$$
\mathbb{P}(y_i=1|\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb{P}(0< y_i^*),
$$
where $y_i^* = \boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i + \varepsilon_i$, with $\varepsilon_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Variable $y_i^*$ can be interpreted as a (latent) variable that determines $y_i$ (since $y_i = \mathbb{I}_{\{y_i^*>0\}}$).

Figure \@ref(fig:Latent) illustrates this situation.

```{r Latent, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="A latent normal index with mean one and variance one. The area to the right of zero is the probability of observing outcome one.", fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, out.width="95%"}
local({
  z <- seq(-3.5,5,length.out=1000)
  par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
  plot(z, dnorm(z,1), type="n", xlab="Latent index", ylab="Density",
       ylim=c(0,.46), las=1)
  for (positive in c(FALSE,TRUE)) {
    v <- if (positive) seq(0,5,length.out=400) else seq(-3.5,0,length.out=400)
    polygon(c(v,rev(v)), c(dnorm(v,1),rep(0,length(v))),
            col=if(positive) "#B5DAE0" else "#F0D3BE", border=NA)
  }
  lines(z, dnorm(z,1), lwd=2, col="#334155")
  abline(v=0, col="#334155")
  abline(v=1, col="#147D92", lty=2)
  text(-1.6,.27,"Outcome 0\nProbability 0.159", cex=.9)
  text(2.9,.27,"Outcome 1\nProbability 0.841", cex=.9)
  text(1,.44,"Mean = 1", cex=.9)
})
```


Assume that agent ($i$) chooses $y_i=1$ if the utility associated with this choice ($U_{i,1}$) is higher than the one associated with $y_i=0$ (that is $U_{i,0}$). Assume further that the utility of agent $i$, if she chooses outcome $j$ ($\in \{0,1\}$), is given by
$$
U_{i,j} = V_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j},
$$
where $V_{i,j}$ is the deterministic component of the utility associated with choice and where $\varepsilon_{i,j}$ is a random (agent-specific) component. Moreover, posit $V_{i,j} = \boldsymbol\theta_j'\bv{x}_i$. We then have:
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbb{P}(y_i = 1|\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta) &=& \mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol\theta_1'\bv{x}_i+\varepsilon_{i,1}>\boldsymbol\theta_0'\bv{x}_i+\varepsilon_{i,0}) \nonumber\\
&=& F(\boldsymbol\theta_1'\bv{x}_i-\boldsymbol\theta_0'\bv{x}_i) = F([\boldsymbol\theta_1-\boldsymbol\theta_0]'\bv{x}_i),(\#eq:utility)
\end{eqnarray}
where $F$ is the c.d.f. of $\varepsilon_{i,0}-\varepsilon_{i,1}$.

Note that only the difference $\boldsymbol\theta_1-\boldsymbol\theta_0$ is identifiable (as opposed to $\boldsymbol\theta_1$ *and* $\boldsymbol\theta_0$). Moreover, replacing $U$ with $aU$ ($a>0$) gives the same model; this *scaling* issue can be solved by fixing the variance of $\varepsilon_{i,0}-\varepsilon_{i,1}$.

:::{.example #migration name="Migration and income"}

The RUM approach has been used by @Nakosteen_Zimmer_1980 to study migration choices. Their model is based on the comparison of marginal costs and benefits associated with migration. The main ingredients of their approach are as follows:

* Wage that can be earned at the present location: $y_p^* = \boldsymbol\theta_p'\bv{x}_p + \varepsilon_p$.
* Migration cost: $C^*= \boldsymbol\theta_c'\bv{x}_c + \varepsilon_c$.
* Wage earned elsewhere: $y_m^* = \boldsymbol\theta_m'\bv{x}_m + \varepsilon_m$.

In this context, agents decide to migrate if $y_m^* >  y_p^* + C^*$, i.e. if
$$
y^* = y_m^* -  y_p^* - C^* =  \boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x} + \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{=\varepsilon_m - \varepsilon_c - \varepsilon_p}>0,
$$
where $\bv{x}$ is the union of the $\bv{x}_i$s, for $i \in \{p,m,c\}$.
:::


## Alternative-varying regressors {#Avregressors}

When attributes such as fares and travel times vary across alternatives, specify utility for each available choice.

For instance, let $\bv{u}_{i,j}$ collect the fare and travel time of alternative $j$ for traveller $i$, while $\bv{v}_i$ collects characteristics of the traveller. A specification with common coefficients on alternative attributes is
$$
V_{i,j}={\theta^{(u)}}'\bv{u}_{i,j}+{\theta_j^{(v)}}'\bv{v}_i.
$$
Taking the difference between utilities gives
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}(y_i=1\mid\bv{x}_i)=F\left({\theta^{(u)}}'(\bv{u}_{i,1}-\bv{u}_{i,0})+
[\theta_1^{(v)}-\theta_0^{(v)}]'\bv{v}_i\right). (\#eq:utility3)
\end{equation}
Thus it is the difference in attributes that enters the binary model.

:::{.example #transport-binary name="Train or bus?"}

Consider a hypothetical journey with the following options:

| Attribute | Train ($j=1$) | Bus ($j=0$) | Train minus bus |
|-----------|---------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Fare (CHF) | 12 | 8 | 4 |
| Travel time (minutes) | 25 | 40 | $-15$ |

A logit specification might assign the train probability
$$
\mathbb{P}(y_i=1)=\Lambda\big(\alpha+\beta_c(c_{i,1}-c_{i,0})+
\beta_t(t_{i,1}-t_{i,0})\big),
$$
where $\Lambda$ is the logistic distribution function. For this journey the index is $\alpha+4\beta_c-15\beta_t$. With negative fare and time coefficients, the higher fare lowers the train probability while the shorter journey raises it. These are illustrative attributes, not an estimated model. Estimation would require observations on choices and on the attributes of **both** available alternatives.
:::

## Estimation {#binary-estimation}

Once the probability function has been specified, its parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood. Each observation contributes the probability assigned to the outcome that actually occurred.

Condition on the covariates and assume independent outcomes across entities. Write $p_i=g(\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i)$. The conditional probability of the observed outcome is $p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}$, giving the log-likelihood
$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
$$
Its score is
$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta}
=\sum_{i=1}^n\bv{x}_i\frac{(y_i-p_i)g'(\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i)}{p_i(1-p_i)}.
$$
Numerical maximization finds the coefficient vector for which this score is zero. In the logit model, $g'=p_i(1-p_i)$, so the score simplifies to $\bv{X}'(\bv{y}-\bv{p})$ and the Hessian is
$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta\partial\boldsymbol\theta'}
=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-p_i)\bv{x}_i\bv{x}_i'.
$$
The log-likelihood is concave. Full column rank gives strict concavity at finite coefficients, but a finite maximum may fail to exist when regressors perfectly separate the two outcomes.

Under the regularity conditions of Section \@ref(secMLE), the MLE is approximately normal with covariance equal to the inverse information matrix. For either link, the conditional expected information is
$$
\bv{I}(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\bv{X})=
\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{[g'(\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i)]^2}{p_i(1-p_i)}
\bv{x}_i\bv{x}_i'.
$$
Evaluating its inverse at the estimates gives an estimated covariance matrix under the specified Bernoulli model.

:::{.example #creditProbit name="Predicting next-month credit defaults"}

We return to `AEC::UCIcredit`, described in Appendix \@ref(data-credit). Each of the 30,000 rows records one cardholder and whether a default payment was recorded in the following month. We ask whether the recorded credit limit, age, and latest repayment status help predict this outcome.

We use three predictors: the log of the credit limit (measured relative to NTD 100,000), age in decades relative to age 40, and an indicator for a **recorded payment delay** in September (`PAY_0 >= 1`). The credit limit is the amount of credit available on the card, not income or the outstanding balance. The comparison group for the delay indicator includes all other repayment codes; some of these codes are undocumented, so it should not be described as a group with no repayment problems.

We randomly reserve 9,000 cardholders for evaluation and estimate all models on the remaining 21,000. The reserved outcomes are used only in Section \@ref(binary-predictions). This split evaluates predictions for other clients in the same collection of observations.

```{r credit-binary-sample}
credit_binary <- transform(AEC::UCIcredit,
  default = default_next_month,
  log_limit = log(LIMIT_BAL / 100000),
  age10 = (AGE - 40) / 10,
  delay = as.integer(PAY_0 >= 1))
training_rows <- sample.int(nrow(credit_binary), 21000)
credit_train <- credit_binary[training_rows, ]
credit_test <- credit_binary[-training_rows, ]
credit_null <- glm(default ~ 1, data=credit_train, family=binomial())
credit_basic <- glm(default ~ log_limit + age10, data=credit_train,
                    family=binomial())
credit_logit <- glm(default ~ log_limit + age10 + delay,
                    data=credit_train, family=binomial())
credit_probit <- update(credit_logit, family=binomial(link="probit"))
```

The same three predictors enter the logit and probit specifications. Table \@ref(tab:credit-binary-coefficients) reports their estimates and standard errors. A positive coefficient raises the predicted probability, holding the other predictors fixed; coefficient magnitudes across links are not directly comparable.

```{r credit-binary-coefficients}
binary_coefficients <- data.frame(
  Predictor=c("Constant", "Log credit limit", "Age (decades)", "Recorded delay"),
  Logit=coef(credit_logit),
  `SE logit`=sqrt(diag(vcov(credit_logit))),
  Probit=coef(credit_probit),
  `SE probit`=sqrt(diag(vcov(credit_probit))), check.names=FALSE)
data_table(binary_coefficients, digits=3, row.names=FALSE,
           caption="Credit-default models: estimates and standard errors (21,000 training observations).")
```

The delay coefficient is positive in both models. The following sections translate this association into probability differences and assess whether it improves predictions.
:::

## Marginal effects {#marginalFX}

The coefficients of probit and logit models affect a latent index, so they are not themselves changes in probability. Marginal effects translate coefficient estimates back into the probability scale and generally depend on the covariate values.

How to measure marginal effects, i.e. the effect on the probability that $y_i=1$ of a marginal increase of $x_{i,k}$? This  object is given by:
$$
\frac{\partial \mathbb{P}(y_i=1|\bv{x}_i;\boldsymbol\theta)}{\partial x_{i,k}} = \underbrace{g'(\boldsymbol\theta'\bv{x}_i)}_{>0}\theta_k,
$$
which is of the same sign as $\theta_k$ if function $g$ is monotonously increasing.

This derivative applies when $x_{i,k}$ enters the index linearly, without transformations or interactions. Two summaries are common: evaluate it at the mean covariate vector (**marginal effect at the means**), or average the individual derivatives (**average marginal effect**, AME). The latter keeps each observation's covariate combination; the former can describe an artificial profile, especially with categorical predictors.

For a binary predictor, use a finite difference instead: predict each observation once with that predictor set to one and once with it set to zero, holding the other predictors fixed, then average the differences. For a transformed continuous predictor, recompute its transformations when changing the underlying variable.

:::{.example #credit-binary-effects name="From coefficients to probabilities"}

In our credit model, the AME of `age10` is the average link derivative times its coefficient. It is a local slope per decade. For the credit limit we instead compare probabilities before and after a 10\% increase, which adds $\log(1.1)$ to `log_limit`. For the delay indicator we compare its two possible values. All three summaries average over the training sample and describe model-implied associations.

```{r credit-binary-effects}
credit_effects <- function(model) {
  eta <- predict(model, newdata=credit_train, type="link")
  base <- predict(model, newdata=credit_train, type="response")
  higher <- transform(credit_train, log_limit=log_limit + log(1.1))
  delayed <- transform(credit_train, delay=1L)
  other <- transform(credit_train, delay=0L)
  c(mean(model$family$mu.eta(eta)) * coef(model)[["age10"]],
    mean(predict(model, higher, type="response") - base),
    mean(predict(model, delayed, type="response") -
         predict(model, other, type="response"))) * 100
}
data_table(data.frame(
  Comparison=c("Age: local slope per decade", "Credit limit: +10%",
               "Recorded delay: 0 to 1"),
  Logit=credit_effects(credit_logit), Probit=credit_effects(credit_probit)),
  digits=2, row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Average changes in predicted default probability (percentage points).")
```

For example, the logit comparison for recorded delay is about `r round(credit_effects(credit_logit)[3],1)` percentage points. A 10\% higher credit limit corresponds to a much smaller change, about `r round(credit_effects(credit_logit)[2],2)` percentage points.

A percentage-point change is a difference between probabilities multiplied by 100; it is not a percentage change in risk. The large contrast for recorded delay summarizes a strong predictive association, rather than the effect of an intervention on repayment behaviour.

Figure \@ref(fig:credit-binary-profiles) illustrates why a single coefficient does not imply a constant probability difference. It holds age at 40 and varies the credit limit and delay indicator.

```{r credit-binary-profiles, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Logit predictions at age 40. Curves differ only in the recorded-delay indicator; the comparison group includes all other repayment codes."}
local({
  limits <- seq(50000,500000,length.out=300)
  profiles <- data.frame(log_limit=log(limits/100000), age10=0, delay=0L)
  p0 <- predict(credit_logit, profiles, type="response")
  profiles$delay <- 1L
  p1 <- predict(credit_logit, profiles, type="response")
  par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
  plot(limits/1000, 100*p0, type="l", col="#147D92", lwd=2,
       ylim=c(0,70), xlab="Credit limit (thousands of NTD)",
       ylab="Predicted default probability (%)", las=1)
  lines(limits/1000, 100*p1, col="#C76D36", lwd=2, lty=2)
  legend("topright", c("Other repayment codes", "Recorded delay"),
         col=c("#147D92", "#C76D36"), lty=1:2, lwd=2, bty="n", cex=.9)
})
```
:::

## Goodness of fit {#binary-fit}

After interpreting individual coefficients, we turn to the performance of the model as a whole. For binary outcomes, fit can be assessed through likelihood-based measures, calibration, and the quality of probability predictions.

McFadden's **pseudo-$R^2$** compares the maximized log-likelihood $\widehat\ell$ with that of an intercept-only model, $\widehat\ell_0$, on the same observations:
$$
R^2_{MF}=1-\frac{\widehat\ell}{\widehat\ell_0}.
$$
A value of zero means that the fitted model does no better in likelihood terms than the constant-probability benchmark. This measure is not a fraction of variance explained and does not evaluate predictions on new observations.

:::{.example #credit-binary-fit name="Does repayment status add information?"}

We compare the intercept-only logit model, the model with credit limit and age, and the model that also includes recorded delay.

```{r credit-binary-fit}
credit_fits <- list("Constant only"=credit_null,
                    "Limit + age"=credit_basic,
                    "Limit + age + delay"=credit_logit)
data_table(data.frame(
  Specification=names(credit_fits),
  `Log-likelihood`=vapply(credit_fits, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m)), 0),
  `Pseudo-R2`=vapply(credit_fits, function(m)
    1-as.numeric(logLik(m)/logLik(credit_null)), 0), check.names=FALSE),
  digits=c(0,1,3), row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Within-sample fit of nested logit specifications.")
credit_LR <- 2*as.numeric(logLik(credit_logit)-logLik(credit_basic))
credit_LR_p <- pchisq(credit_LR, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE)
```

Adding recorded delay gives a likelihood-ratio statistic of `r round(credit_LR,1)`. Against the $\chi^2_1$ reference distribution, the p-value is below 0.001: delay contributes information conditional on limit and age. Section \@ref(binary-predictions) checks predictions on reserved observations.
:::

## Predictions and ROC curves {#binary-predictions}

A predicted probability becomes a classification only after a threshold is chosen. ROC curves summarize the trade-off between true- and false-positive rates across all possible thresholds, separating the model's ranking ability from any single decision rule.

To classify an outcome, choose a threshold $c$ and set $\widehat y_i=1$ when $\widehat p_i\geq c$. A lower threshold detects more positive outcomes but also produces more false alarms. The appropriate trade-off depends on the consequences of the two mistakes.

The **receiver operating characteristic (ROC)** curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as the threshold varies:
$$
\mathrm{TPR}=\frac{\text{correctly flagged positives}}{\text{all positives}},
\qquad
\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{\text{incorrectly flagged negatives}}{\text{all negatives}}.
$$
A threshold above every score gives $(0,0)$; one below every score gives $(1,1)$. Random ranking has a diagonal ROC in expectation. The **area under the curve (AUC)** measures ranking quality: it is the probability that a randomly selected positive receives a higher score than a randomly selected negative, counting ties as one half.

Ranking is only one aspect of a probability forecast. **Calibration** asks whether outcomes occur at the predicted frequencies: among observations assigned a probability near 0.2, approximately one fifth should have outcome one. The **Brier score**, $n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\widehat p_i)^2$, assesses probability accuracy; smaller values are better.

:::{.example #credit-binary-predictions name="Evaluating predictions for reserved cardholders"}

We now predict outcomes for the 9,000 cardholders excluded from estimation. The benchmark assigns every client the default share in the training sample. None of these models is refitted on the evaluation sample.

```{r credit-binary-predictions}
credit_test_predictions <- data.frame(
  Benchmark=rep(mean(credit_train$default), nrow(credit_test)),
  Logit=predict(credit_logit, credit_test, type="response"),
  Probit=predict(credit_probit, credit_test, type="response"))
credit_auc <- function(y, p) {
  n1 <- sum(y==1); n0 <- sum(y==0)
  (sum(rank(p, ties.method="average")[y==1])-n1*(n1+1)/2)/(n1*n0)
}
data_table(data.frame(
  Model=names(credit_test_predictions),
  Brier=vapply(credit_test_predictions, function(p)
    mean((credit_test$default-p)^2), 0),
  AUC=vapply(credit_test_predictions, function(p)
    credit_auc(credit_test$default,p), 0)),
  digits=3, row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Probability accuracy and ranking on 9,000 reserved observations.")
```

Both fitted models reduce the Brier score relative to the constant-probability benchmark. Their AUC is about `r round(credit_auc(credit_test$default,credit_test_predictions$Logit),2)`: they rank defaults above non-defaults more often than chance, while leaving substantial uncertainty. The two links give similar predictive performance. Their ROC curves and the logit's calibration plot appear in Figure \@ref(fig:credit-binary-validation). A good ranking does not guarantee calibration: the left panel compares clients with one another, while the right panel compares probabilities with observed frequencies.

```{r credit-binary-validation, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.8, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Evaluation on reserved observations. Left: ROC curves for logit and probit. Right: observed default frequencies against average logit predictions in ten equally sized groups ranked by predicted probability. The diagonal represents perfect calibration."}
local({
  par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4.3,4.3,2,1), mgp=c(2.7,.8,0))
  plot(c(0,1),c(0,1),type="n",xlab="False-positive rate",
       ylab="True-positive rate",las=1,main="Ranking")
  abline(0,1,col="#CBD5E1",lty=3)
  for (j in 1:2) {
    p <- credit_test_predictions[[j+1]]
    # Aggregate ties before accumulating counts: one ROC point per distinct score.
    counts <- rowsum(cbind(positive=credit_test$default,
                         negative=1-credit_test$default), group=-p, reorder=TRUE)
    lines(c(0,cumsum(counts[,"negative"])/sum(counts[,"negative"])),
          c(0,cumsum(counts[,"positive"])/sum(counts[,"positive"])),
          col=c("#147D92","#C76D36")[j],lty=j,lwd=2)
  }
  legend("bottomright",c("Logit","Probit"),col=c("#147D92","#C76D36"),
         lty=1:2,lwd=2,bty="n",cex=.9)
  p <- credit_test_predictions$Logit
  group <- ceiling(rank(p, ties.method="first")/900)
  calibration <- aggregate(cbind(predicted=p, observed=credit_test$default),
                           list(group=group),mean)
  plot(calibration$predicted,calibration$observed,pch=19,col="#147D92",
       xlim=c(0,.8),ylim=c(0,.8),xlab="Average predicted probability",
       ylab="Observed default share",las=1,main="Calibration")
  abline(0,1,col="#CBD5E1",lty=3)
})
```

Finally, consider two illustrative logit thresholds, 0.5 and 0.2. They are specified for comparison, rather than selected to maximize performance on the reserved outcomes.

```{r credit-binary-classification}
credit_classification <- do.call(rbind,lapply(c(.5,.2), function(cutoff) {
  flagged <- credit_test_predictions$Logit >= cutoff
  y <- credit_test$default
  data.frame(Threshold=cutoff, TP=sum(flagged & y==1),
             FP=sum(flagged & y==0), FN=sum(!flagged & y==1),
             TN=sum(!flagged & y==0),
             TPR=mean(flagged[y==1]), FPR=mean(flagged[y==0]))
}))
data_table(credit_classification, digits=c(1,0,0,0,0,3,3),row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Logit classifications: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), and true negatives (TN).")
```

Lowering the threshold detects more defaults and flags more clients who do not default. Overall classification accuracy alone can be misleading: predicting no default for everyone would already be correct for `r round(100*mean(credit_test$default==0),1)`\% of these clients, while detecting none of the defaults. The table makes both types of error visible.
:::

## Chapter recap {#binary-recap}

::: {.recapbox data-latex=""}

- The LPM can give predictions outside $[0,1]$ and requires robust inference. Probit and logit use bounded probability functions (Figure \@ref(fig:LPM)).
- Latent indices and utility differences motivate binary-choice models; alternative-specific attributes enter through utility comparisons (Sections \@ref(latent) and \@ref(Avregressors)).
- Maximum likelihood estimates index coefficients. Derivatives and finite differences translate them into probability comparisons (Sections \@ref(binary-estimation) and \@ref(marginalFX)).
- Within-sample fit, ranking, calibration and classification answer different questions. Reserved observations assess predictive performance (Sections \@ref(binary-fit) and \@ref(binary-predictions)).

:::
